name: Priya Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a callout electrician for Brightline Services, so I fix things that break in restaurants, cafés and shops around the city. A dispatcher sends jobs to my phone: a fryer that keeps tripping, a walk-in fridge with no power, emergency lights failing their test. Some days it's five jobs, some days it's one long one in a basement.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy walking into a kitchen where the chef is shouting and leaving it quiet and working, that's a good feeling. What wears me out is the late calls, a restaurant losing power at nine at night on a Saturday. I'm paid well with the overtime, I own a flat with a small mortgage, and I've got about eight months saved, which my mother says is still not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I've never trusted the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a fashion, like every other one, and that the people who kept their heads did fine. I'd say it at family dinner mostly, my uncles love talking about this. I'd keep it short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes very little. Brightline already uses a computer to send jobs to my phone, and if that gets a bit smarter, fine. A fridge with no power still needs someone with a meter and a screwdriver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my callouts and keep paying extra off the flat, about two hundred a month on top. I'd keep helping at my parents' bakery on Sunday mornings, they rely on me for their ovens. And I'd probably start my master electrician's course next year, since it means better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the life I've already got, and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your mother says eight months isn't enough. What does she mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother thinks a woman on her own should have a year saved and the flat paid off before thirty. She's not wrong, she ran the bakery through two bad years. So I'd keep pushing the savings up even in this world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Arjun (who's studying accounting) worries me more than my own job. He's in his second year and every lecturer talks about software doing the books. But in this picture he'll probably be fine.

say: I'd say AI was a **fashion**, and people who kept their heads did fine.
I'd mostly say it at **family dinner**, with her uncles.
think: Privately, little changes; the dispatch system just gets **a bit smarter**.
A fridge with no power still needs **a meter** and a screwdriver.
do: Pay about **two hundred extra** a month off the flat.
Keep fixing the **bakery ovens** on Sunday mornings.
Start a **master electrician's** course next year for better pay.
feel: **Calm**, because it is the life she already likes.
S0.quote: A fridge with no power still needs someone with a meter and a screwdriver.
fieldNote: Her caution comes partly from her **mother**, who ran a bakery through bad years.
Her outside worry is her brother **Arjun**, an accounting student.
The master's course is about **pay**, not fear of AI.

steps.text: Pay about two hundred a month extra off the flat mortgage
Keep doing callouts for Brightline as now
Enrol in the master electrician's course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds closer to what my brother keeps telling me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say trades are holding up and families should stop pushing every child into a desk job. I'd say it at the temple and to my cousins, a few of them are in offices. I'd probably repost something about apprenticeships too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my own work is mostly safe, the fixing part needs hands. But Brightline's dispatchers and the woman who writes up the invoices would probably go, and the system might start telling me exactly which job, which route, how long. I'd keep my job, but it would feel more like being a machine's arms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the dispatch app properly, since the firm will push it, and I'd ask for training on the new diagnostic kit if they bring it in. I'd do the master electrician's course, because if Brightline gets squeezed the qualified people stay. And I'd tell Arjun to add a trade or practical skill to his degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, more for the office people and for Arjun than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother Arjun to do a bookkeeping job with real clients on weekends, not just exams. Or come with me on callouts in the summer and learn some wiring, it never hurts. He'll roll his eyes, but he'll listen to Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a machine's arms'. What would that mean on a normal day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the app decides I go to the café before the restaurant, and times how long I take. Right now I use my head, I know which chef will keep me talking for twenty minutes. I don't want to lose that judgement, it's half the job.

say: I'd say trades are **holding up** and families should stop pushing desk jobs.
I'd say it at the **temple** and to her cousins in offices.
think: Brightline's **dispatchers** and invoice clerk would probably go.
She'd keep her job but feel like **a machine's arms**.
do: Learn the **dispatch app** properly and ask for diagnostic kit training.
Take the **master electrician's** course to stay among the kept.
Tell Arjun to add a **practical skill** to his degree.
feel: **A little uneasy**, mostly for office colleagues and Arjun.
S1.quote: I'd keep my job, but it would feel more like being a machine's arms.
fieldNote: Her worry is about **losing judgement** at work, not losing the job.
She thinks being **qualified** protects her if the firm is squeezed.
Family is her main **sounding board**: mother, brother, cousins.

steps.text: Learn Brightline's dispatch app and new diagnostic tools
Persuade Arjun to do weekend bookkeeping with real clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a big claim. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's wait and see, because people have said big things before. In public I'd keep calm, especially around my parents, they'd panic. I'd say a trade still has years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared for Arjun first, he'd finish his degree right as accounting disappears. Then by 2031 a robot that can fix a fryer is a robot that can do my callouts. I'd be thirty-two, with a flat, and I'd need a plan by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare penny into the mortgage and savings, aiming for the flat clear by 2031. I'd do the master electrician's course quickly, because someone still has to sign off and take legal responsibility. And I'd look hard at whether the bakery could use me full time, a family business with regulars might last longer than a callout firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be counting months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents' bakery really last longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure. People still like a real baker they know by name, but robots could bake too, eventually. It's a place to stand, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, for racing ahead without thinking about families. And governments, for letting them. I believe in business, but a good business doesn't wreck its own customers.

say: I'd say **wait and see**, because big claims have come before.
I'd stay calm in public to avoid **panicking** her parents.
think: Her brother Arjun would graduate just as **accounting disappears** in 2028.
By **2031** robots could do all her callouts, when she is thirty-two with a flat.
do: Put every spare penny into **mortgage and savings**, flat clear by 2031.
Rush the **master electrician's** course for legal sign-off work.
Look at working **full time** in the family bakery.
S2.quote: A robot that can fix a fryer is a robot that can do my callouts.
fieldNote: Her **public calm** hides real private fear.
She thinks the **family bakery** might outlast a callout firm, but isn't sure.
She blames **big tech and governments**, while staying pro-business.

steps.text: Pay off the flat mortgage by 2031
Finish the master electrician's course within a year
Ask her parents about working full time at the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels more like real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, and that the trades should be in charge of training, not the tech companies. I'd say it at the temple and to the lads at Brightline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years means Arjun has time to change course, and I'd have until about 2034 on callouts. That's enough to clear the flat and get qualified up. What I don't know is what a master electrician does when robots do the work. Maybe I.d supervise them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's course in the first year and then ask Brightline about a supervisor role. I'd put more into the flat but not stop living. And I'd help my parents get their ovens and wiring modern now, so the bakery is in good shape for whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see a path. I like having a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once I see the other sparkies using them properly. If an app helps me find faults faster, I'll use it. I just don't want to be the first one to trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother the flat will be paid off in four years and I'll be a supervisor. She'd ask about marriage next, she always does. But that's a different interview.

say: I'd say there's **time to get ready**.
I'd say the **trades** should run the training, not tech firms.
think: She'd have until about **2034** on callouts, time to clear the flat.
She isn't sure what a **master electrician** does once robots work.
do: Finish the **master's course** and ask about a **supervisor** role.
Pay more off the **flat** without stopping living.
Modernise her parents' **ovens and wiring** now.
S3.quote: What I don't know is what a master electrician does when robots do the work.
fieldNote: She is steady: she'll use AI **once others prove** it.
Her plan is to move **up**, to supervisor, rather than out.
Her **family** keeps pulling her back to marriage and security.

steps.text: Apply for a supervisor role at Brightline after qualifying
Rewire and modernise the bakery ovens this year
Overpay the flat mortgage to clear it in four years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people who keep working and saving will be fine. I'd say young people should still learn a trade, it'll just change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2039 I'd be forty, with the flat paid off and maybe a family of my own. That's a good position. I'd want to be supervising or inspecting by then, not crawling under shop counters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Brightline and do the master's course next year. I'd learn the new tools as they come, a few years behind the keenest ones. And I'd keep saving steadily, the flat first, then something for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. It's on my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If I marry, I'd still want children, maybe around thirty-two. Ten years is enough to be settled first, that's how my parents did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young people at the temple?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young people at the temple to learn a trade and keep learning, because the trade will change. And to save, even a little. That's what worked for my family.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** for people who keep working and saving.
I'd say young people should **still learn a trade**.
think: By 2039 she'd be forty with the **flat paid off**.
She'd want to be **supervising or inspecting**, not crawling under counters.
do: Carry on at **Brightline** and take the master's course next year.
Learn **new tools** a few years after the keenest.
feel: **Mostly calm**, on her mind but not keeping her up.
S4.quote: I'd want to be supervising or inspecting by then, not crawling under shop counters.
fieldNote: Ten years fits her **traditional plan**: settle first, then family.
She sees the trade **changing**, not ending.
Her advice to others mirrors her **own habits**: work and save.

steps.text: Take the master electrician's course next year
Keep saving each month towards paying off the flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Arjun and I would both be hit within a few years, and my parents would worry themselves sick. What would help is a clear route for qualified electricians into supervising and inspecting, and honest advice for students like Arjun before they finish degrees that go nowhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how families talk about it. My uncles think trades are forever, my brother thinks everything is over. The truth is probably in the middle, and you just keep working.

headlineQuote: My uncles think trades are forever, my brother thinks everything is over.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old callout electrician** fixing restaurant and shop faults, owning a flat with eight months saved.
She is **traditional and steady**, guided by her mother and her family's bakery.
Her outside worry is her brother **Arjun**, an accounting student facing AI.
In the AGI pictures she plans to clear the flat and move up to **supervisor or inspector**.
She keeps a **calm public face** while privately counting months in the fast picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with her callouts and Arjun's future hit within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear route** into supervising and inspecting.
**Honest advice** for students before they finish degrees.
